segments.title: Judge frigates by the missions they must perform
segments.body: A warship's value depends on the job its navy expects it to do. River-class offshore patrol vessels illustrate the point: they suit presence, diplomacy, and maritime security, while a high-threat battle would demand a different ship. A modern frigate can support a screen and perform picket duties, although a destroyer is more likely to be built as the task group's principal screening asset. Missile-cell counts alone do not settle that classification: a ship can be built to destroyer standards and receive only a minimal VLS fit. Light frigates occupy another tier because their cost, weapons, and wartime assumptions differ from those of larger frigates. The comparison follows the requirements that produced each class instead of trying to name one universal winner.

evidence.note: The introduction defines the comparison by mission and contrasts OPVs, light frigates, frigates, and destroyer screening roles.

segments.summary: Compare frigates by their missions, their place in a fleet, and the level of combat they must survive.

segments.title: Type 26 as a specialist submarine hunter
segments.body: Type 26 begins with a clear purpose: finding and killing submarines before they can attack a task group. Submarines are dangerous because they can approach unseen, yet history also shows that dedicated surface and air ASW forces can destroy them. The escort must protect troop transports, supply ships, and carriers whose combined value far exceeds the frigate's own price. That requirement explains why a first-rate submarine hunter cannot be treated as a cheap platform. Rafted machinery, hull shaping, sensors, and accumulated ASW experience all serve the same specialist mission.

evidence.note: The lecture identifies Type 26 as an ASW specialist and links its cost and design measures to the submarine threat.

segments.summary: Type 26 is an expensive ASW specialist built to defend task groups against equally costly and capable submarines.

segments.title: Why does a specialist ASW frigate cost so much?
segments.body: A nuclear submarine costing around a billion pounds is the price comparison used here. Hunting that submarine requires an escort capable of confronting a threat built to a similarly demanding standard. The frigate must also protect the task group's movement of troops and supplies, along with its carrier's air power. The argument is that this defensive responsibility makes an equally serious investment in ASW capability necessary.

evidence.note: A reported recurring question about the price of these frigates is answered through the approximate billion-pound submarine comparison and the escort's responsibility for the task group.

segments.summary: A costly submarine threat and the task group's defensive needs explain the investment in a specialist ASW frigate.
segments.question: Why does a specialist ASW frigate such as Type 26 cost so much?
segments.answerShort: It must match the capability of an expensive submarine while protecting the troops, supplies, and carrier air power moving with its task group.

segments.title: City, River, and Hunter variants in allied task groups
segments.body: Every Type 26 variant must defend itself and contribute outside ASW, even though submarine hunting remains its foundation. The Royal Navy's City class can rely on carrier-group aircraft and Type 45 destroyers for much of the outer air-defence battle. Canadian River-class destroyers and Australian Hunter-class frigates face a broader integration problem because they may join British, American, Japanese, or other allied formations. Their wider capabilities help them reinforce both ASW and air defence when the composition of the allied formation changes. Canada could also assemble surface action groups, although that is considered unlikely here. Its planned River order is described as potentially larger than the British City and Australian Hunter orders combined, with the eventual comparison dependent on Norwegian orders and changes to British plans. The variants show how coalition expectations can reshape a common hull without erasing its original purpose.

evidence.note: The passage compares City, River, and Hunter requirements, the uncertain relative size of national orders, and the different expectations of allied task-group service.

segments.summary: The British, Canadian, and Australian Type 26 variants adapt one ASW-centered design to different assumptions about task-group support and coalition service.

segments.title: Type 26 as the task group's ASW director
segments.body: Type 26 is cast as the ASW equivalent of the air-defence ship that directs a task group's wider defensive picture. Its own sensors and quieting give it first-rate hunting ability, while its larger role is to coordinate other ships and aircraft. Uncrewed systems extend that network under the frigate's direction. This arrangement brings separate search assets into one submarine-hunting effort across the formation.

evidence.note: The lecture compares Type 26 with an air-defence director and says it should see and direct the task group's ASW assets, including uncrewed systems.

segments.summary: Type 26 is meant to coordinate a task group's ships, aircraft, and uncrewed systems as well as hunt submarines with its own sensors.

segments.title: How NATO escort groups reinforce carrier formations
segments.body: Carrier and amphibious ships usually provide the large command facilities around which allied task groups are assembled. Standing NATO maritime patrols and surface action groups can themselves be led by an escort. In this interpretation, those groups also provide additional escorts for carrier formations in the Atlantic or Mediterranean. Cost-cutting is suggested as the reason carrier groups have too few escorts permanently attached, creating a need to assemble reinforcements.

evidence.note: The lecture distinguishes carrier and amphibious command ships from escort-led NATO groups, then links reinforcement of carrier screens to reduced escort numbers and savings.

segments.summary: Standing NATO maritime groups can operate under an escort's command and later add ships to a carrier group's screen.

segments.title: How Type 26 is arranged around ASW sensors
segments.body: The weapons occupy a limited part of the layout, while the stern carries a large flight deck, hangar, and mission bay for crewed or uncrewed ASW assets. The discussed British fit lacks the dedicated shipboard torpedo launchers often expected on an ASW frigate; such launchers would normally fire the same class of lightweight torpedo carried by the helicopter. Hull form keeps the flow around the bow-mounted Type 2150 sonar as clean as possible. The Type 2087 towed array is expected to do much of the searching, alongside the bow sonar and information from other ships and aircraft. Computer space, cooling, and electrical power matter because modern ASW depends on combining several streams of acoustic data. Rafted machinery and electric motors reduce the ship's own noise. Quieting also makes the frigate harder to detect, while its primary benefit here is allowing the sonars to hear weak submarine signatures through less self-generated interference.

evidence.note: The lecture connects the mission bay, aviation facilities, Type 2150 and Type 2087 sonars, computing, and quiet propulsion to the ASW mission.

segments.summary: The flight deck, mission bay, sonars, computing spaces, and quiet propulsion plant reveal how deeply ASW shapes the Type 26 layout.

segments.title: FREMM modularity and the Constellation redesign problem
segments.body: FREMM was conceived as a modular, adaptable frigate family that customers could configure for different mission mixes. That flexibility still assumes users will work with the interfaces and modules built into the design. The US Constellation program illustrates the consequences of replacing those modules with American equipment and reconfiguring the ship around it. Even air-conditioning units of roughly the same size can put their intake hoses and power connections in different places. Rerouting those services for one substitution after another can turn individually modest changes into a substantial redesign of the ship.

evidence.note: The passage introduces FREMM modularity and explains how changed equipment interfaces accumulated in the Constellation redesign.

segments.summary: FREMM offers an adaptable base design, while Constellation shows how national substitutions can turn small interface changes into a major redesign.

segments.title: FREMM trades some ASW specialization for breadth
segments.body: FREMM retains a strong ASW capability, but its French and Italian requirements spread design effort across more jobs. A rough comparison rates Type 26 as a 90 percent ASW solution and FREMM as a 75 to 80 percent solution that can also reach about 70 percent across other missions. Those figures are illustrative judgments rather than test scores. They explain why a navy seeking one balanced ship may prefer FREMM, while a force with separate air-defence and strike assets can afford a more focused Type 26. Portugal is given as an example of a customer that needs a broad, practical capability from each hull.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts Type 26 specialization with FREMM's broader French and Italian general-purpose requirements.

segments.summary: Type 26 concentrates on ASW, while FREMM accepts a lower peak in that specialty to remain useful across a wider set of missions.

segments.title: Why FREMM attracted so many national variants
segments.body: FREMM can patrol dispersed territories, support fire missions, hunt submarines, contribute to air defence, and enter contested waters without needing an entire task group beside it. Its firepower is intended to get the ship itself into and out of difficult situations; protecting an entire formation is a larger requirement. The Italian variants make that flexibility especially visible through their layered weapons. The program snapshot gives 66 planned ships across several customers, 27 French and American cancellations, and 22 active hulls. Orders were still evolving, so the figures describe the position presented in this comparison. The design's appeal comes from a sound common base that can accept different national priorities. Conceptually, it is a higher-end development of the MEKO approach to modular warship families.

evidence.note: The passage covers FREMM mission breadth, national orders and cancellations, and its relationship to modular design families such as MEKO.

segments.summary: A useful core hull, adaptable mission fit, and credible independent capability made FREMM attractive to navies with very different patrol and combat needs.

segments.title: FREMM weapon layers, firing arcs, and redundancy
segments.body: In this interpretation, Type 26 and FREMM reflect an era when Western navies expected technological superiority and more freedom to choose their wars. Their limited VLS capacity and uneven defensive layers still carry that assumption, although the Italian FREMM fit closes more of the gaps. It combines missiles, a five-inch gun, 76 mm guns, and 25 mm weapons so threats can be engaged at several ranges. Layering also provides alternatives when one system fails or exhausts its ammunition. A fore-and-aft pair with roughly 270-degree arcs can retain coverage of much of the ship after one mount fails, while a pair on opposite sides with 180-degree arcs can leave one side undefended. Three or four suitably placed mounts give more overlap. Guns and future laser systems need an unobstructed line of sight, so the proposed design sequence fixes their positions first. Vertical-launch missiles can turn after launch, giving designers more freedom to place their cells once the direct-fire arcs are protected.

evidence.note: The lecture uses Italian FREMM layers to explain system availability, overlapping coverage, firing arcs, and VLS placement.

segments.summary: The Italian FREMM fit introduces a wider design lesson: limited magazines expose earlier threat assumptions, while overlapping gun arcs and redundant layers keep defensive options available.

segments.title: Project 17 frigates for independent Indian operations
segments.body: Project 17 develops through the Shivalik class, Project 17A Nilgiris, and the planned Project 17B ships. Indian planning begins with the expectation that the navy may have to operate alone, while allied help remains useful when available. That assumption pushes each frigate toward a flexible mix of self-defence, task-group support, and offensive reach. The ships can reinforce carrier or surface groups and also conduct visible deployments across the Indian Ocean and farther abroad. Each generation reduces acoustic, infrared, and other signatures while increasing capability. The line has also moved from Indianized versions of Russian design ideas toward a recognizable national style, strengthening the ships' value for overseas presence.

evidence.note: The passage traces Project 17 development and links Indian frigate design to independent operations and wider power projection.

segments.summary: Shivalik, Nilgiri, and the planned Project 17B form an iterative frigate family shaped by India's need to operate without assuming allied support.

segments.title: Project 17B ambitions and the Indian frigate weapons mix
segments.body: Project 17B is described as a planned third iteration of approximately 8,000 tons with about 48 vertical-launch cells. A more heavily armed alternative would start frigates around 64 cells, destroyers around 128, and cruisers closer to 192; these are personal armament preferences. The wider Project 17 family discussion includes BrahMos anti-ship missiles and the Indian-Israeli Barak 8 air-defence system. The existing eight-weapon BrahMos load prompts a recommendation to raise that to at least 16 while carrying 48 Barak weapons. The gun and close-in fit combines an OTO Melara 76 mm weapon with AK-630 mounts. RBU-6000 launchers add options in shallow water against submarines or uncrewed threats, while torpedoes and a shipboard helicopter extend the ASW layer. A suggested heavier fit would also have three each of the 76 mm and AK-630 systems to improve coverage and resilience. These recommendations describe a preferred future fit rather than an approved configuration.

evidence.note: The lecture gives Project 17B size and VLS estimates, personal magazine-size preferences, the existing Indian weapons mix, and a proposed heavier future fit.

segments.summary: An estimated 8,000-ton Project 17B provides a starting point for examining the Indian frigate family's missiles, guns, and ASW weapons, alongside proposals for a heavier fit.

segments.title: AK-630 traverse limits and overlapping close defence
segments.body: A well-maintained AK-630 can put a large volume of fire into the direction of an incoming threat, and the Indian mounts are reported to receive that care. Its elevation range is recalled as roughly -12 to +88 degrees, with the figures given from memory. Traverse is described as 180 degrees to either side of the normal position, giving full bearing coverage without continuous rotation. Crossing the traverse stop to engage another target can therefore require a long slew around the opposite way. Goalkeeper and Oto Melara's 40 mm system are cited as alternatives with continuous 360-degree traverse. A possible AK-630 modification for continuous rotation is mentioned, but whether it has entered use remains uncertain. Multiple mounts can compensate for the stop and preserve overlapping coverage. A preference for at least three mounts follows from that concern about target switching and redundancy.

evidence.note: The passage qualifies the remembered AK-630 elevation and traverse figures, compares continuous traverse on Goalkeeper and an Oto Melara 40 mm system, and explains why additional mounts are preferred.

segments.summary: A gun can cover every bearing without rotating continuously; AK-630, Goalkeeper, and an Oto Melara 40 mm system illustrate why traverse limits matter when switching targets.

segments.title: Indian ASW helicopters and the cost of learning
segments.body: India operates domestically developed helicopters and Sea King variants. An EH101 or new-build Merlin purchase remains an uncertain possibility. A Merlin-sized aircraft may suit an Indian doctrine that gives the helicopter more independence during submarine prosecution, requiring more computing capacity and mission equipment aboard the aircraft itself. In this comparison, Russian practice relies more heavily on several aircraft working together, while American helicopters remain closely integrated with their ships. An indigenous replacement would face the mistakes and compromises of a first domestic generation. A technology can be mature internationally and still be first-generation work for a particular national industry. Designs that look sound on paper can reveal problems as that industry gains experience building and operating them. Licensed production offers one route to learning the manufacturing process and design philosophy before attempting a fully national successor.

evidence.note: The passage compares ASW helicopter operating concepts and explains first-generation indigenous development and licensed-production learning.

segments.summary: A possible Merlin fit leads into the doctrine, onboard computing, and industrial learning needed for India to field an independent ASW helicopter capability.

segments.title: Three heavy-frigate design philosophies
segments.body: The three larger frigate families embody different design priorities. Type 26 is the dedicated ASW specialist. FREMM keeps a strong submarine-hunting capability inside a wider general-purpose package. The Nilgiri and Project 17 line adds industrial development, using successive ships to build India's national design and construction base.

evidence.note: The lecture explicitly summarizes Type 26, FREMM, and Nilgiri as products of three different design priorities.

segments.summary: Type 26 prioritizes ASW, FREMM balances several missions, and the Nilgiri family couples combat capability with growth of India's national naval industry.

segments.title: Mogami's path from compact destroyer to light frigate
segments.body: Japan began the program in 2015 while seeking a new compact destroyer. By August 2026, ten Mogamis are counted as in service, with two more expected before March 2027. That is a rapid construction pace even when the full development period is included. At roughly 4,000 tons standard displacement, the ship falls into the modern light-frigate tier used in this comparison. A patrol vessel handles constabulary work without a frontline warfighting fit, while a corvette is a combatant intended for shorter deployments. A light frigate is the smallest combatant expected to deploy for extended periods and fight within a task group or under land-based cover. Mogami replaces older Asagiri and Abukuma destroyer escorts by adding affordable hulls to larger Japanese formations.

evidence.note: The passage dates the Mogami program, gives its recording-date service count, defines the light-frigate category, and identifies the classes it replaces.

segments.summary: The Mogami program began in 2015 as a compact destroyer effort and settled into a light-frigate role that supplies deployable wartime mass.

segments.title: What separates a light frigate from a corvette or patrol ship?
segments.body: The distinction used here starts with what the ship must do in wartime. A patrol ship lacks the combat fit expected of the other two categories. A corvette can fight, but its role does not call for weeks or months of distant deployment. A light frigate is the smallest combatant in this classification expected to combine that endurance with wartime operations. It is intended to work with the larger ships of a task group or within reach of land-based forces, rather than act as a detached wartime picket. Mogami illustrates the role by replacing older destroyer escorts and adding hulls to a formation.

evidence.note: The lecture explicitly repeats a frequently asked question about light frigates, corvettes, and patrol ships, then answers it through combat fit, endurance, and task-group or land-based support.

segments.summary: Combat equipment, deployment endurance, and expected support distinguish the three categories in this comparison.
segments.question: What is the difference between a light frigate, a corvette, and a patrol ship?
segments.answerShort: An OPV handles patrol duties without a frontline warfighting fit. A corvette is armed for war but intended for shorter deployments. A light frigate combines sustained deployment with combat service alongside a task group or land-based support.

segments.title: Mogami's balanced fit and resistance to feature creep
segments.body: Mogami uses a conventional propulsion plant, while its compact integrated mast is singled out as an innovative feature that has attracted interest from India and other navies. Its standard fit includes 16 Mark 41 cells, which could hold 64 quad-packed Evolved Sea Sparrow Missiles or a smaller number of larger weapons. Eight Type 17 anti-ship missiles continue Japan's domestic, iterative missile-development path. Mine-laying equipment, torpedoes, a helicopter, and a five-inch gun cover a wide range of fleet and peacetime work. In role and philosophy, the ship resembles an Oliver Hazard Perry or MEKO 200 updated for current threats. Adding every desirable weapon would quickly increase size and cost, so the existing restraint is part of the design's value.

evidence.note: The lecture reviews Mogami's mast, VLS, missiles, mine and ASW equipment, and the need to control feature growth in a light frigate.

segments.summary: Sixteen Mark 41 cells, Type 17 missiles, mine equipment, torpedoes, a helicopter, and a five-inch gun give Mogami broad utility without turning it into a larger frigate.

segments.title: Japan's iterative route to domestic anti-ship missiles
segments.body: Japan's anti-ship missile capability grew through repeated domestic development. The earlier stage is recalled as Type 88 or SSM-1, associated with work in the 1980s and ideas reaching back into the 1970s. The later Type 12 provides another example of continued development, while Mogami carries eight Type 17 missiles. American systems remain part of the picture through purchases, adaptation, and domestic manufacture.

evidence.note: The lecture links Mogami's Type 17 missiles to an iterative Japanese development effort, recalls Type 88 or SSM-1 and its 1970s-1980s origins, mentions Type 12, and discusses using and adapting American systems.

segments.summary: Mogami's Type 17 missiles sit within a Japanese effort to develop domestic weapons through successive designs while continuing to use and adapt American systems.

segments.title: Upgraded Mogami missile capacity and Australian choices
segments.body: The upgraded design rises to about 4,800 tons standard and 6,200 tons fully loaded while retaining similar engine power. Its Mark 41 battery doubles to 32 cells, enough for 128 ESSM if every cell carries four missiles. Japan's Type 23 surface-to-air missile is a domestic option that appears unable to quad-pack, leaving at most 32 such missiles before cells are assigned to rocket-assisted torpedoes or other weapons. ESSM and CAMM show how quad-packing could provide greater defensive depth through a domestic development or an overseas purchase. Cooperation with Britain and Italy on a fighter project is suggested as one possible opening for CAMM cooperation, with no decision assumed. The Japanese fit is expected to retain Type 97 torpedoes and domestic anti-ship missiles; a five-inch gun is anticipated despite a preference for 76 mm. The Australian fit is expected to use ESSM and may add a RIM-116 Rolling Airframe Missile system. The design remains an adaptable lower-tier escort whose customer can trade domestic content against magazine capacity.

evidence.note: The passage gives upgraded Mogami displacement and VLS figures, then compares Japanese domestic missile and Australian quad-packed options.

segments.summary: The enlarged Mogami doubles Mark 41 capacity to 32 cells, opening different Japanese and Australian choices about domestic missiles, quad-packing, guns, and close defence.

segments.title: Mogami supplies mass in Japan's high-low fleet mix
segments.body: Japan already has top-tier Aegis destroyers, with larger Aegis ships under construction, and a middle band of other destroyers. Mogami can therefore concentrate on the lower escort tier. More hulls spread the formation, provide mutual support, and keep useful ships available in several places at once. Requiring every escort to match a Maya or Kongo would shrink the fleet through cost. The resulting high-low mix balances combat quality with the number of ships needed for routine deployments and wartime depth. Continuous construction also preserves yard skills and avoids the expense of repeatedly restarting production. Australian and other export interest strengthens that industrial logic by extending the run.

evidence.note: The lecture places Mogami in Japan's lower escort tier and connects fleet mass with continuous shipyard production and exports.

segments.summary: Japan can field affordable Mogamis in numbers because larger Aegis ships cover the top tier and steady yard work lowers the cost of replacing the rest of the force.

segments.title: The uneasy symbolism of HMS Campbeltown
segments.body: The Inspiration-class naming scheme is meant to connect each Type 31 with an aspect of Royal Navy history. HMS Campbeltown represents amphibious forces through a destroyer remembered for blowing itself up during an important World War II operation. The choice prompts a personal reservation: that successful wartime sacrifice can seem an awkward association for a new ship intended to support amphibious forces. Other raids and participating ships, including those associated with Operation Claymore, offered different naming possibilities.

evidence.note: The lecture questions Campbeltown as an amphibious-forces name and contrasts its wartime sacrifice with other raid histories.

segments.summary: Naming a Type 31 after HMS Campbeltown recalls a destroyer's deliberate wartime sacrifice, an association that draws a personal objection.

segments.title: Type 31 as the task group's defensive goalkeeper
segments.body: Arrowhead designs are named for their approximate length, with the Type 31 derived from the Arrowhead 140 family. The British fit functions as a flak frigate or goalkeeper near the carrier or amphibious ship. A 57 mm gun, two 40 mm guns, and a large short-range missile load can engage threats that penetrate the outer screen. Mark 41 cells can accommodate Tomahawk and other strike weapons, while the anticipated British load emphasizes quad-packed CAMM alongside some cruise missiles. That defensive profile also suits forward presence because it creates a substantial obstacle without presenting the same offensive concentration as a strike-heavy combatant. In a task group, its job is to preserve the protected ship after the longer-range layers have already fired.

evidence.note: The passage explains Arrowhead naming and presents Type 31 as a short-range defensive layer for carriers, amphibious ships, and forward presence.

segments.summary: The British Type 31 fit emphasizes short-range missiles and medium guns, making it a final defensive layer around a carrier or amphibious ship.

segments.title: Arrowhead's export appeal is space for adaptation
segments.body: Arrowhead 120, 140, and the discussed 160 variant use numbers corresponding to their approximate intended lengths. Even the 140 family allows variation, with hull lengths described as roughly 137 or 140 metres depending on the customer. Poland and Indonesia can use the available space for their own sensors, weapons, accommodation, and future changes. The design is compared with a practical van because the customer receives a sound platform with a large usable interior. Relatively small crews reduce the recurring personnel burden. Efficient construction and open volume make the family attractive to navies that want to shape a ship around their own requirements.

evidence.note: The lecture explains Arrowhead length designations, including the 137-140 metre variation and the discussed 160 option.
The lecture links Polish and Indonesian interest to Arrowhead hull space, adaptability, crew efficiency, and buildability.

segments.summary: Polish and Indonesian interest reflects Arrowhead's large hull, moderate crew needs, and room for national weapons and later upgrades.

segments.title: How stop-start orders slow British frigate production
segments.body: Changing government decisions appear to be the main production problem. British yards can assemble ships quickly, but revised requirements may force completed work to be undone and rebuilt. Slow funding then stretches a small order so the yard does not finish years before the next program is ready. Full-rate Type 26 production could absorb Norwegian ships with much less disruption, although the first Norwegian delivery might still require transferring a British construction slot. The workforce would face a sharp fall once the run ended without enough successor work. The apparent cancellation of the Type 83 plan adds uncertainty, with its possible revival left open. Regular orders would let yards build faster while retaining the people and facilities needed for the next class.

evidence.note: The passage connects British schedule changes, low order volume, Norwegian Type 26 slots, and workforce continuity to slow, costly production.

segments.summary: British yards can build faster, but changing requirements and too few follow-on orders force slow production that protects workforces at a higher unit cost.

segments.title: StanFlex, MEKO, and two kinds of modularity
segments.body: Arrowhead builds on the capable Iver Huitfeldt design and its Danish experience with StanFlex. StanFlex modules can be craned off and replaced, with reconfiguration described as taking a day or less. Denmark retained the concept and is pursuing a newer version, despite limited success selling it abroad. MEKO succeeded with a different promise: customers begin with a common core design and choose modules while the ship is being designed and built. Other attempts at rapid in-service reconfiguration have struggled despite strong interest in modular language. Light frigates would benefit most from genuine mission changes because they provide numbers and adaptable space. Suggested uses include mine-laying, mine-sweeping support, amphibious support, and extra boats for operations against piracy or drug smuggling. Those are possibilities for adaptable ships, while the delivered platforms mainly provide space and dependable propulsion, power, command, and sensor systems.

evidence.note: The lecture compares StanFlex module swaps, MEKO design-stage customization, and the unrealized value of in-service modularity for light frigates.

segments.summary: The Iver Huitfeldt lineage contrasts StanFlex's rapid in-service module swaps with MEKO's more commercially successful design-stage customization.

segments.title: FDI combines combat utility with visible presence
segments.body: Vehicle analogies separate the three light-frigate approaches. Type 31 is the spacious van, Mogami is the flexible estate car, and FDI is the more purposefully arranged saloon. Mogami reduces radar signature through conventional stealth shaping, while FDI also creates an unmistakable visual identity. That visibility supports port visits and global French presence because observers can recognize the ship immediately. Combat utility remains central, and the distinctive silhouette gives the ship additional status. That combination helps explain why other navies see FDI as a route to fleet capability and a prominent national presence.

evidence.note: The passage uses vehicle analogies to distinguish Type 31, Mogami, and FDI, then links FDI's visual character to presence and export value.

segments.summary: FDI's distinctive silhouette supports French overseas presence and export efforts alongside its combat role.

segments.title: French, Greek, and Swedish FDI missile fits
segments.body: The French baseline uses two eight-cell Sylver A50 launchers for 16 Aster 15 or Aster 30 missiles. The final two French ships are expected to gain another 16 cells for a total of 32. Sweden's Luleå variant is planned with 24 CAMM-ER weapons and 24 Aster 30s, creating a 48-missile air-defence load. The Greek configuration carries 24 Aster cells and another eight A70 cells for land-attack cruise missiles. A50 is the tactical-length launcher, while A70 provides the longer strategic cell. These differences show how one compact hull can be adapted around national ideas of local air defence, Baltic operations, and strike capability.

evidence.note: The lecture compares French, Swedish, and Greek FDI missile-cell counts and distinguishes Sylver A50 and A70 lengths.

segments.summary: One FDI hull supports markedly different French, Greek, and Swedish missile magazines, ranging from compact Aster fits to mixed CAMM, Aster, and strike-length cells.

segments.title: FDI gun fits, order totals, and French program cost
segments.body: The French and Greek versions use the OTO Melara 76 mm gun, while Sweden keeps its Bofors tradition with 57 mm and 40 mm weapons. The plans recalled here total five French, four Greek, and four Swedish ships. That produces only 13 hulls despite the design's export success, a total considered too small in this assessment. The five-ship French program is estimated at about 3.5 billion euros including development, or roughly 700 million euros per ship in 2025 money. Construction accounts for 2.1 billion euros and development for 1.4 billion, so comparisons need to separate recurring hull cost from one-time design expense. Sweden's Luleå variant includes substantial changes and should be treated as a modified design when comparing its cost and capability with the French baseline.

evidence.note: The passage lists national gun fits, planned hull totals, and the French construction and development cost breakdown.

segments.summary: The French FDI program averages about 700 million euros per ship including development; the orders described total 13 ships with different national gun fits.

segments.title: FDI as a Baltic principal combatant and export demonstrator
segments.body: Swedish FDI-derived ships are expected to act as principal surface combatants in the Baltic, especially because the navy will operate only a small number. A recognizable and visibly capable ship can carry diplomatic weight when it enters a port or appears during a regional operation. France has reinforced that effect by sending an in-service FDI to visit potential customers and demonstrate the design. Greece's Kimon also gives buyers a second operational national variant to examine. Being able to tour and inspect a working ship can change how procurement teams judge a design. Mogami and FDI have gained an advantage in competitions where they could appear in service while Type 31 remained a paper or building-stage offer.

evidence.note: The lecture identifies the in-service French Amiral Ronarc'h and Greek Kimon as tangible examples that can be shown to potential customers.
The closing comparison links Swedish Baltic duties and warship appearance with French and Japanese use of in-service ships during export campaigns.

segments.summary: Sweden can use its FDI-derived frigates as principal Baltic combatants, while France demonstrates how an in-service ship can strengthen diplomacy and export campaigns.
